sections.h: The comfort of 4:13-18 in its setting
sections.b: Paul's best-known passage on the Lord's coming was written to a church that had just buried some of its members. He tells them the dead will rise first and the living will be caught up with them, and he ends: "So comfort one another with these words" (4:18). The passage is best read with that purpose in view.

sections.h: A church founded in a hurry (1 Thessalonians)
sections.b: 1 Thessalonians shows the church Paul left behind in the city: converts who had turned from idols (1:9), suffered from their own countrymen (2:14), worked with their hands (4:11) and were known across Macedonia and Achaia for their faith (1:7-8). Paul had been driven out (Acts 17:10) and wrote to them from Corinth after Timothy's visit.
sections.refs: 1 Thessalonians 1:7-9; 1 Thessalonians 2:14; 1 Thessalonians 2:17; 1 Thessalonians 3:1-6; 1 Thessalonians 4:11; Acts 17:1-10

sections.b: 1 Thessalonians, probably written about AD 50 from Corinth, shows Paul early in his mission: working with his hands to support himself (2:9), writing as one of a team with Silvanus and Timothy, longing for converts he was forced to leave (2:17-3:10), and picturing himself as their nurse and their father (2:7, 11). It also has some of his sharpest words about his Judean opponents (2:14-16).

The letter opens "From Paul, Silvanus and Timothy" (1 Thessalonians 1:1), so the whole letter speaks as "we," with Paul's own "I" breaking in only at 2:18, 3:5 and 5:27. Silvanus had helped found the church (Acts 17:4, 10) and had been driven out with Paul. His name at the head of the letter tells the converts that all three men they knew stand behind its comfort and its commands. When Paul says "we" were "treated with insults at Philippi" (2:2), Silvanus is one of the "we": Acts says he was beaten and jailed there with Paul (Acts 16:19-24).

sections.b: Paul sent Timothy from Athens to strengthen the young church in Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3:1-5) and calls him "our brother, who works together with God in the good news about Christ" (1 Thessalonians 3:2; some manuscripts read "God's servant"). Timothy's return with good news of their faith and love is the occasion of 1 Thessalonians (3:6).

sections.h: The first written words on the Lord's coming
sections.b: 1 Thessalonians is probably the earliest Christian writing to speak of Jesus' parousia, "coming" (2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23). New believers were taught to "wait for his Son to come from the heavens" (1:10). Paul describes the Lord coming down from heaven with a shout, an archangel's voice and God's trumpet, the dead in Christ rising, and the living caught up to meet him (4:16-17), and he warns that the day will come like a thief (5:2).
sections.refs: 1 Thessalonians 1:10; 1 Thessalonians 2:19; 1 Thessalonians 3:13; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18; 1 Thessalonians 5:1-11; 1 Thessalonians 5:23

common: Paul's word for the Lord's coming, parousia, was also used of a ruler's official visit to a city.
uncommon: Some scholars think 5:1-11 was added later to correct the hope of 4:13-18.

sections.b: "Next, we who are alive and remain will be caught up along with them in clouds, to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thessalonians 4:17). The Greek harpazo, "snatch up," is rapiemur in the Latin Vulgate, the source of the word "rapture." The passage was written to comfort mourners (4:13, 18). Whether the meeting is a separate event before a tribulation or part of Christ's one return is the dividing question; the card on 1 Thessalonians 4 sets the churches' answers side by side. The word "meeting" (apantesis) was read by John Chrysostom as citizens going out to welcome a king.

common: Pre-tribulation teaching takes 1 Thessalonians 5:9 ("God did not appoint us to face anger") as a promise that the church will be removed before the tribulation.
uncommon: Some read the meeting in the air as an escort: believers go out to meet the Lord and return with him to earth, as a city met a visiting ruler.

sections.h: The dead in Christ will rise first (1 Thessalonians 4)
sections.b: Paul's earliest surviving word on the resurrection answers grief: believers who have died will not miss the Lord's coming, because "if we believe that Jesus died and rose," God will bring them with him, and "Those who are dead in Christ will rise first" (1 Thessalonians 4:14, 16). Paul develops the teaching in 1 Corinthians 15.

Paul calls dead believers "those who have fallen asleep" (1 Thessalonians 4:13-15) and says that, "whether we stay awake or sleep," believers "live in company with him" (5:10). The sleep image was common for death among Greeks and Jews (Daniel 12:2). The churches read it differently: as a picture of the body's rest while the soul is with Christ, or (as Seventh-day Adventists teach) as an unconscious state until the resurrection.

sections.h: Like a thief at night (1 Thessalonians 5)
sections.b: Paul takes up the prophets' "day of the LORD" and makes it the day of the Lord Jesus: it "is coming the way a thief comes at night" (1 Thessalonians 5:2), with sudden ruin for those who say "Peace and safety" (5:3). Believers, "sons of light and sons of day," need not be caught by surprise (5:4-5).

1 Thessalonians uses orge three times: Jesus "rescues us from the anger that is coming" (1:10); "the anger has reached" those who block the mission to Gentiles (2:16); and "God did not appoint us to face anger" but salvation (5:9). The anger is the judgment of the day of the Lord.

Paul compares the Thessalonians' persecution by their own countrymen with that of the Judean churches by "the Jews, who killed the Lord Jesus as well as the prophets" (1 Thessalonians 2:14-15). Read in its setting, this is a Jew's angry polemic about Judean opponents of the mission. Later Christians used it, with Matthew 27:25, to blame the Jewish people as a whole. Some scholars think the verses were added after AD 70 (Pearson, 1971); most hold them to be Paul's. Gilliard (1989) argued that the comma after "the Jews" makes the words sound general.

Some scholars hear in "Peace and safety" (1 Thessalonians 5:3) an echo of Rome's boast of peace and security (Weima, 2012); others doubt that the pair was a Roman slogan in Paul's day (White, 2013) and point to the false prophets' "Peace, peace" (Jeremiah 6:14). The church's founding riot in Thessalonica turned on the charge of proclaiming "another king" (Acts 17:7).

Paul describes Gentile conversion in one sentence: "you turned away from idols to God, to serve a God who lives and is true" (1 Thessalonians 1:9). For people in a Greek city, that meant leaving family rites, civic festivals and guild meals, which helps explain their troubles (1:6; 2:14).

"God's will is this: your being made holy" (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Paul applies Israel's call to holiness (Leviticus 19:2) to Gentile converts, first in sexual life (4:3-8), and prays that God will make them "holy in every part," spirit, soul and body (5:23).

Paul's earliest teaching on sexual ethics tells Gentile converts to keep away from porneia, to gain control of one's own "vessel" (body or, some say, wife) in holiness, and not to wrong a brother. The Jerusalem letter used the same verb (Acts 15:29).

sections.h: Quiet lives and working hands (1 Thessalonians)
sections.b: Paul worked "night and day" so as not to burden the church (1 Thessalonians 2:9) and urges the believers to live quietly and work with their hands so that they need no one (4:11-12), and to set straight those "out of line" (5:14). 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12 takes up the same problem.

Paul prays "without a break" for the church (1 Thessalonians 1:2-3; 3:10) and asks the same of it (5:17). Augustine read the command as continual desire for God (Letter 130); in the Orthodox East it shaped the practice of the Jesus Prayer and the story The Way of a Pilgrim.

sections.h: Do not snuff out the Spirit (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21)
sections.b: Paul's earliest word on the gifts is a balance: "Do not snuff out the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies as nothing. Instead, put everything to the test, and keep hold of what is good" (1 Thessalonians 5:19-21). The Catholic Catechism cites the passage on testing charisms (801).

In the church at Thessalonica people spoke prophecies; Paul tells the church not to scorn them but to test them (1 Thessalonians 5:20-21), as he tells Corinth to let others "weigh what is said" (1 Corinthians 14:29).

Paul says the Lord will come down "with an archangel's voice" (1 Thessalonians 4:16). He names no angel; the only archangel named in the Bible is Michael (Jude 1:9), whom Daniel ties to the time when the dead wake (Daniel 12:1-2).

The Lord's coming is announced "with God's trumpet" (1 Thessalonians 4:16), as Sinai was (Exodus 19:16) and as the great horn gathers the scattered (Isaiah 27:13). 1 Corinthians 15:52 calls it "the last trumpet."

Paul tells former idol worshipers, "we know that you are chosen" (1 Thessalonians 1:4), and gives as evidence the power of the message among them and their joyful faith under pressure (1:5-6). He also says God did not "appoint" them to anger but to salvation (5:9).

Paul counts himself among "we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord" (1 Thessalonians 4:15, 17). Many scholars think he expected to live to see it; others read "we" as "whoever of us is alive." In the same letter he refuses to name a date (5:1-2).

sections.h: The first sketch of the armor (1 Thessalonians 5:8)
sections.b: Before Ephesians 6, Paul dresses believers in God's armor from Isaiah 59:17: "the breastplate of faith and love, and let the hope of salvation be our helmet" (1 Thessalonians 5:8).

One Greek letter separates nepioi, "infants," from epioi, "gentle," at 1 Thessalonians 2:7. NA28 prints "infants" with Papyrus 65, Sinaiticus as first written and Vaticanus; the SBL and Tyndale House editions print "gentle" with Alexandrinus and the Byzantine text. The case shows how a single letter can split the editions.

sections.h: A church "in God the Father" (1 Thessalonians 1:1)
sections.b: In what is probably his first surviving letter, Paul calls the believers of one city "the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (1 Thessalonians 1:1), using the word for a city's civic assembly. He compares them with "God's churches that are in Judea" (2:14), and asks them to respect those who "stand at your head in the Lord" (5:12).
